title: Alka Yagnik Received the Padma Bhushan on Sunday. She Has Been Losing Her Hearing Since 2024. She Sang the Songs That Every NRI Plays at Every Wedding, Every Road Trip, Every Moment of Homesickness.
excerpt: The voice behind 'Taal Se Taal Mila,' 'Ek Do Teen,' and an entire generation's emotional memory of India was honoured at Rashtrapati Bhavan. She could barely hear the applause.
body:
Every NRI household has the same invisible guest: Alka Yagnik's voice. It is there when the uncles take over the Bluetooth speaker at Diwali. It is there in the car on the way to the temple. It is the first song at every sangeet, the last song at every garba night, the one that plays on loop when homesickness wins at 2 AM in a studio apartment in New Jersey.

On Sunday, May 25, 2026, President Droupadi Murmu conferred the Padma Bhushan — India's third-highest civilian honour — on Alka Yagnik at Rashtrapati Bhavan in New Delhi. She walked up to accept it in the same ceremony where Hema Malini received Dharmendra's posthumous Padma Vibhushan in tears, where Mammootty was honoured with his own Padma Bhushan, and where R Madhavan, Prosenjit Chatterjee, and dozens of others received recognition for lifetimes of work.

But Alka Yagnik's moment carried a weight that the others did not.

## The Diagnosis That Changed Everything

In June 2024, Yagnik revealed publicly that she had been diagnosed with a rare form of sensorineural hearing loss. The condition, which she attributed to a viral attack, had significantly diminished her ability to hear — a devastating blow for a woman whose entire life has been built on sound. She disclosed the diagnosis on Instagram with a simple post that asked fans to avoid loud music and take care of their ears.

The music industry responded with an outpouring of support. AR Rahman, Sonu Nigam, and Kumar Sanu all publicly expressed solidarity. But for the millions of Indians and NRIs who grew up on her voice, the news felt personal in a way that celebrity health announcements rarely do.

## A Career Measured in Collective Memory

The numbers are staggering even by Bollywood standards. Yagnik has recorded over 10,000 songs across a career spanning four decades. She has won seven Filmfare Awards for Best Female Playback Singer — a record that stood for years. Her collaborations with composers like AR Rahman, Jatin-Lalit, Anu Malik, and Nadeem-Shravan produced some of the most recognisable melodies in Indian pop culture history.

But the real measure of her career is not awards or numbers. It is ubiquity. "Taal Se Taal Mila" from *Taal*. "Ek Do Teen" from *Tezaab*. "Kuch Kuch Hota Hai" from the film of the same name. "Gali Mein Aaj Chand Nikla" from *Zakhm*. "Kajra Re" from *Bunty Aur Babli*. "Didi Tera Devar Deewana" from *Hum Aapke Hain Koun*. These are not just songs. For the Indian diaspora, they are coordinates on a map of emotional memory — each one marking a wedding, a birthday party in a rented community hall, a midnight FaceTime call with a grandmother who cannot work the volume button.

## The Diaspora Angle Nobody Talks About

Here is what makes Yagnik's honour resonate differently outside India: she never crossed over. She never tried to become a global brand. She never sang in English or collaborated with Western artists for crossover appeal. She was, and remains, relentlessly, unapologetically Hindi film music.

And that is precisely why NRIs hold her close. In a world where every Indian cultural export now comes packaged for global consumption — where yoga is Lululemon and butter chicken is a Whole Foods frozen meal — Alka Yagnik's voice is the thing that stayed exactly as it was. It did not need to be translated, remixed, or explained. It just needed to be played.

For first-generation immigrants, her songs were the bridge between the country they left and the one they were building in. For second-generation kids, they were the sound of the household — as much a part of the furniture as the steel thali and the pressure cooker.

## What Comes Next

Yagnik has not announced a retirement. She has spoken about adapting to her condition and continuing to work where possible. The Padma Bhushan is recognition for a body of work that is already complete in its impact, even if new songs remain possible.

At the ceremony, she said simply: "I really want to thank all my listeners."

She could have said more. She did not need to. Every NRI in the world already knows exactly what she has done for them. They hear it every time someone plays "Tujhe Dekha To" at a Fourth of July party and the whole room goes silent for exactly one bar before everyone starts singing along.

That silence, and then that singing — that is Alka Yagnik's legacy.

*Sources: LatestLY, Storyboard18, GlamSham, AIR News, NRI Page*
